extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians, aspiring mathematicians, and educated readers interested in the nature and evaluation of mathematical work
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing what makes mathematical work valuable (beauty, seriousness, permanence, originality), and advising on the proper motives, career timing, and distinctions between types of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as the primary test
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty is the first test: there is no permanent place in the world for ugly mathematics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical work must be aesthetically pleasing: ideas must fit together harmoniously. The aesthetic appeal is comparable to beauty in poetry or painting and is a key determinant of lasting value. Anti-pattern: producing 'ugly' mathematics will not attain permanent place or high regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness / importance of the theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mathematics is 'serious' as well as beautiful; seriousness lies in the significance of the mathematical ideas which a theorem connects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theorem is 'serious' if it connects significant ideas in a natural and illuminating way; such connections tend to lead to important advances in mathematics and other sciences. Anti-pattern: clever or intricate results (e.g., chess problems) that do not connect to broader mathematical complexes are 'trivial' and lack true seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance defined by connectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical idea is 'significant' if it can be connected, in a natural and illuminating way, with a large complex of other mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure significance by how naturally an idea links to many other ideas and whether it opens routes to further development. Examples: theorems by Pythagoras, Euclid, Newton which connect widely. Scoring note: breadth and depth of connections are indicators of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence / endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical achievement has a character of permanence; mathematical ideas wear less with time than words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that remains intelligible and influential across centuries (e.g., Greek mathematics, Archimedes) is evidence of permanence. Preference is given to results whose relevance or internal beauty survives historical changes in language and fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is a creative subject; original ideas and discoveries constitute the proper function of a mathematician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable work introduces genuinely new ideas or viewpoints. Creative output (new theorems, novel techniques) is the main measure of a mathematician's success. Anti-pattern: polishing or routine work without original insight is of lesser value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and elegance of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The form and method of proof (for example, reductio ad absurdum) are part of mathematical excellence; elegant methods are prized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy, clarity, and conceptual neatness in proofs are valued; certain classical proof techniques are celebrated as fine mathematical weapons. Anti-pattern: proofs that are needlessly convoluted, obscure, or lack conceptual insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'real' and 'trivial' mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two mathematics: the 'real' mathematics of professional, creative work (art-like and often not directly useful) and the 'trivial' mathematics (useful, applied, often dull).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real mathematics must be justified as an art (aesthetic and serious), while trivial mathematics is often practically useful (e.g., ballistics). This distinction affects how one defends the subject and evaluates work: aesthetic and conceptual depth mark 'real' mathematics; practical applicability marks 'trivial' mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness is not the primary value measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the best mathematics is not directly useful; practical usefulness is not the chief criterion of mathematical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge mathematical worth primarily by immediate practical applications. A useful but 'dull' applied result is of a different category than deep theoretical results which may be presently 'useless' yet valuable in other respects. Anti-pattern: elevating practical utility above conceptual depth when assessing 'real' mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmlessness and wartime effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Real mathematics has no effects on war; trivial/applied mathematics may facilitate modern warfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing social harm, distinguish branches: pure (real) mathematics is largely harmless and can be an intellectual refuge, whereas applied branches (ballistics, aerodynamics) have direct military applications and moral implications. Use this distinction when weighing ethical consequences of research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate motives for research
rubrics_metrics.description: The dominant incentives to research are intellectual curiosity (desire to know the truth), professional pride (craftsman's shame at unworthy work), and ambition (desire for reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These motives are legitimate and provide the force behind substantial research. Skeptical of claims that primary motive is to 'benefit humanity'; such altruistic motive is rarely the principal driver. Guidance for producers: cultivate curiosity, pride in craft, and ambition as healthy drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and timing: mathematics as a young person's game
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics, more than other arts or sciences, is largely a young man's game; major creative advances are rarely initiated past middle age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the peak period for original contributions to be in youth and early middle age; plan career and ambitions accordingly. Anti-pattern: assuming late age will produce major original breakthroughs is unlikely; later career contributions often involve polishing or exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and talent alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: A gift for mathematics is a highly specialized talent; if one is a real mathematician, one's mathematics will be far better than anything else one can do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals should cultivate their genuine talents rather than attempting second-rate work in other fields. For career choices, prioritize work that matches one's real abilities; sacrifice for talent cultivation is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear standards for recognition and fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics has unusually clear-cut and unanimously accepted standards; those who are remembered are almost always the men who merit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition and lasting fame in mathematics are generally meritocratic: quality of results and conceptual contribution determine remembrance. Use the consensus standards of importance, elegance, and significance when assessing peers and historical figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of collaboration and training others
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration with gifted peers and training other mathematicians are important contributions to mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions include enabling others' work and collaborative achievements (Hardy cites his collaborations with Littlewood and Ramanujan). Mentoring and joint work can extend one's impact beyond individual theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recreational/elementary problems vs professional theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Recreational problems (chess problems, puzzles) are genuine mathematics but tend to be 'trivial'—ingenious but unimportant—whereas professional theorems have broader significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize genre differences: puzzles provide aesthetic pleasure and intellectual 'kick' and have public appeal, but they are of a lower order in terms of long-term mathematical importance. Use different evaluative standards for recreational vs research mathematics.
